# Best open-ear earbuds for running

The review sites agree on a few top picks. I only have the review pages, not direct product pages, so the links go to the reviews, which have the current buy buttons.

| Need | Pick | Price | Key specs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Best overall (sound) | Bose Ultra Open Earbuds | $199 (down from $299) | Clip-on, 7 hr (19.5 with case), IPX4 |
| Best bone conduction | Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 | $180 list, about $125 at some retailers | Neckband, 12 hr, IP55 |
| Best for long or wet runs | Shokz OpenDots 2 | $200 | Clip-on, 10 hr (40 with case), IP57 |
| Best value | Nothing Ear (Open) | about $99 | IP54 |
| Cheapest way to try the style | JLab Flex Open | about $40 | Clip-on, 7 hr, IPX55 per JLab |

**Why these**
- **Bose Ultra Open:** Runner's World named it best overall. It has clear sound, a comfortable fit that doesn't bounce, and little sound leakage. WIRED likes the physical buttons, which are easier to use mid-run. The downsides are the price, IPX4 water resistance (not ideal for heavy rain), and volume that can feel low in loud traffic. Runner's World also says Bose plans to release a new pair soon, so you may want to wait or watch for discounts. ([Runner's World](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/g63667125/best-open-ear-headphones-for-running/), [WIRED](https://www.wired.com/story/best-open-earbuds/))
- **Shokz OpenRun Pro 2:** This is the pick if hearing your surroundings is your top priority. It has more bass than older bone-conduction models and physical controls. WIRED found slightly less clarity than the older OpenRun and the Bose. The neckband can clash with long hair and hoods. ([WIRED review](https://www.wired.com/review/review-shokz-openrun-pro-2/), [RTINGS comparison with the Bose](https://www.rtings.com/headphones/tools/compare/bose-ultra-open-earbuds-shokz-openrun-pro-2-bone-conduction/50264/72946))
- **Shokz OpenDots 2:** WIRED's top overall pick. It has the best battery and water resistance of the group, and it leaves the top of your ear free for glasses and hats. It's pricey, and Runner's World noted the volume could be better. ([WIRED](https://www.wired.com/story/best-open-earbuds/))
- **Nothing Ear (Open):** SoundGuys picked it as best overall and best for running, with strong bass for the category and a good app EQ. ([SoundGuys](https://www.soundguys.com/best-open-ear-headphones-and-earbuds-115102/))

**Budget options**
- **JLab Flex Open (about $40):** Sound is less detailed than pricier pairs, but it's a low-risk way to see if clip-ons work for you. Runner's World's text mentions both $40 and $50, so check the price at checkout.
- **Soundpeats PearlClip Pro (about $50):** WIRED's budget pick. ([WIRED](https://www.wired.com/story/best-open-earbuds/))
- **Soundcore AeroFit 2:** It has an ear hook, IP55, and 10 hr battery. SoundGuys lists it at $79.99 on Amazon, while a deals site shows $129.99 at Soundcore's store, or about $104 with code AFSC20. Those prices conflict, so compare before buying. [Soundcore store link](https://dealectric.com/go/soundcore-aerofit-2) (an affiliate link that opens Soundcore's official US store).

**Tips**
- Open-ear buds leak sound and won't block noise. They're best outdoors, not in a noisy gym.
- Keep the volume low enough to hear traffic.
- For a secure fit, hooks and neckbands (AeroFit 2, OpenRun Pro 2) are the most stable. Clip-ons (Bose, OpenDots 2) are the most comfortable.

If you tell me your budget, whether you run in the rain, and whether you wear glasses or have long hair, I can narrow this to one pick.
